title: KINCHO: Early Mosquito Incense Lasted 40 Minutes. Why Was a Spiral Not Enough?
description:
KINCHO recalls its early straight mosquito incense sticks burning out in about 40 minutes. Why wasn't coiling them into a spiral enough? Follow a surviving wooden mold, extrusion equipment for hand rolling and later die-cutting machines to see how a coil faced the challenges of burning longer, manufacturing and shipping. Historical scenes are original conceptual illustrations; numbers and processes are explained in the period to which each source belongs.

chapters.c05r001: One Stick Ends, Night Goes On

c05r001.text: You want a mosquito incense stick to last the night, but an early one burned out in about 40 minutes.

c05r002.text: Imagine only ash left by the table, with darkness outside. You need another stick; the night has barely begun.

c05r003.text: A spiral wooden mold dating to 1895 seems to give a long stick a circle to hide in.

c05r004.text: But what I find strange is that imagining this circle did not mean it could become a product.

c05r005.text: Another surviving tool later put two long strands into workers' hands. The problem was not over.

c05r006.text: Let's follow KINCHO incense from the table to the factory, and see how a shape survives making and shipping.

c05r007.text: Why was a spiral still not enough for it to burn long and reach the shelf intact?

c05r008.text: The material first had to become something you could hand to a buyer; Eiichiro Ueyama initially received only seeds.

c05r009.text: KINCHO's later timeline starts this journey with an agreement to exchange seeds and seedlings in 1885.

c05r010.text: The next year, seeds sent by an American plant merchant included pyrethrum. The new material had arrived.

c05r011.text: But a packet of seeds on the counter does not give a buyer a usable mosquito incense stick.

c05r012.text: First the flowers had to be grown and harvested. But how could a bowl of powder become something you could light?

c05r013.text: The timeline records the first harvest and trial milling in 1887. Flowers became powder, but not yet a product.

c05r014.text: Only here did I realize how many steps still lay between this worktable and the familiar spiral.

c05r015.text: How were mosquitoes dealt with before? KINCHO's museum recalls burning plants and using smoke to repel them.

c05r016.text: The museum also says people had to boost the smoke when the plants burned vigorously; more smoke could also fill the room.

c05r017.text: The next challenge for those flower seeds was finding another product shape for the powder.

c05r018.text: In 1888, Ueyama shared lodgings in Tokyo with a stick-incense merchant and began another trial.

c05r019.text: The company timeline says he used imported flea powder and a bamboo tube to make mosquito incense; that record does not give the powder's formula.

c05r020.text: Stick incense offered a route: shape powder into a thin strand, giving it a form that could keep burning.

c05r021.text: By 1890, the timeline finally records a straight-stick product going on sale. Seeds had become something sellable.

c05r022.text: But once it reached the table, one stick did not last long. Would making it longer help?

c05r023.text: The company recalls sticks about 20 centimeters long; several often had to be used at once.

c05r024.text: Lighting more sticks gives you more burning points, but does not lengthen the path along any one stick.

c05r025.text: Another problem came before delivery: the maker's factory account says thin, straight sticks broke easily in transit.

c05r026.text: To make a longer stick without needing a longer table, where could that thin strand go?

c05r027.text: Coil it into a circle. KINCHO's later account attributes the idea to Ueyama's wife.

c05r028.text: The company timeline puts the idea and the first trials in that year; this is the company's later attribution.

c05r029.text: Remember the wooden mold at the start? The National Museum of Nature and Science's registry lists it as a prototype.

c05r030.text: Imagine a cord: lay it straight, and the table must make room for its full length.

c05r031.text: Wind it inward, turn by turn: the path still follows the cord, but it takes up less flat space.

c05r032.text: I think this is an elegant turn. But does fitting a small table mean a factory can deliver it?

c05r033.text: The challenge moved: winding one on a table is one thing; a factory must deliver product after product.

c05r034.text: The mold's plan was to fill it with material, then push out a spiral. A shape had become a tool.

c05r035.text: Seeing only the exhibit, you might assume it began mass production. Did it really enter a production line?

c05r036.text: KINCHO's technical heritage page is explicit: the wooden mold was unsuitable for mass production and was never adopted.

c05r038.text: An object proving the idea existed cannot, by itself, prove products were being made in a steady stream.

c05r042.text: What we can follow is the unsolved production problem: the drawing is round, but where is the product?

c05r043.text: Further down the company timeline is a patent filing. Can filing stand in for a product launch?

c05r044.text: At the counter to buy a coil, are you waiting for a product to arrive, or another record on paper?

c05r045.text: No. KINCHO's timeline dates the spiral mosquito incense patent filing to 1900.

c05r046.text: No original application is available to check, so we say filed, without adding that it was granted.

c05r047.text: The actual launch came in 1902, seven years after the spiral idea was proposed.

c05r048.text: Those seven years invite curiosity, but the sources give no year-by-year trial log. We cannot invent a failure for every year.

c05r049.text: I'd rather follow the next surviving tool. How did later workers make those long strands into coils?

c05r050.text: It is an extruder for hand rolling, labeled by the maker as used from around 1910, after the launch.

c05r051.text: Unlike filling a wooden mold, it first extrudes noodle-like strands, then hands them to workers.

c05r052.text: Notice what workers receive: two extruded strands, placed together, then wound by hand around a circle.

c05r053.text: The source page does not say the machine extruded two at once; it confirms two were joined at the hand-rolling step.

c05r054.text: Why did those two spirals have to stay together on their way to the shelf?

c05r055.text: KINCHO says paired coils can reduce breakage in transit and transport costs; no exact savings are given here.

c05r056.text: What interests me is that the same circle began answering another problem: once longer, it still had to arrive whole.

c05r057.text: But staying connected for shipping and how slowly a single coil burns after lighting are different mechanisms.

c05r058.text: So what definite records of length and burn time remain for these later products?

c05r059.text: KINCHO's museum lists a coil from around 1919: about 58 centimeters long, burning for about 6 hours.

c05r060.text: Those are the museum's details for that later product, not the trial mold or the very first launch day.

c05r061.text: The museum also lists a hand-rolled product from around 1922, burning about 12 hours. That is another product.

c05r062.text: These figures belong to different products and periods. Can their hours be converted directly into mosquito-killing power?

c05r063.text: So we cannot divide the later coil's time by the early stick's and call it a multiple of mosquito-killing power.

c05r064.text: The hours measure how long it burns. Hearing them as strength of effect adds a claim to the evidence.

c05r067.text: The hand-rolled circle next met a die-cutting machine. Did workers' hands leave as soon as it was completed?

c05r068.text: Not so neatly. The company timeline says that in 1940, an automatic rotary die-cutting machine for spiral mosquito incense was completed.

c05r069.text: But the surviving hand-rolling equipment's description lists use all the way to around 1957.

c05r070.text: One record says a new machine was completed; another says the old equipment remained in use. They need not hand over on the same day.

c05r071.text: I think this feels like production history: an invention's year rarely holds every production line's later life.

c05r072.text: Beyond the method, raw materials had to hold the shape. What later happened to the flower fields and ingredients?

c05r073.text: Materials changed too. KINCHO's factory account says pyrethrum cultivation shrank to increase food production.

c05r074.text: The same account says the synthetic ingredient allethrin was developed and put into use around 1955.

c05r075.text: That is the maker's account of material development, not a claim that all mosquito incense changed formula that year.

c05r076.text: Next, the timeline records completion of an improved, high-efficiency automatic die-cutter; the factory account also places mechanical die-cutting in this period.

c05r080.text: Back to the paired coils you get today: shipped connected, where should they be separated before use?

c05r081.text: The maker's current Q&A says to press gently in the middle, then pinch the thicker center to separate the coils.

c05r082.text: Pulling hard from the outer edge may break them; if not using them yet, keep them joined to reduce warping.

c05r083.text: You may know the feeling: before even using something, you worry your own hands will break it.

c05r084.text: Separating them only gives each coil its own path. Why can fire travel slowly along it?

c05r085.text: KINCHO's factory explains it through the cross-section: few gaps make it hard for oxygen to enter, so it burns slowly.

c05rx001.text: The maker offers a specific comparison: keep shape, material, thickness and length the same, but reduce the weight.

c05rx002.text: It looks the same outside, but is looser inside. Could air reach the material more easily?

c05rx003.text: The company explains that lower density exposes it to air more easily inside and out, so it should burn faster.

c05rx004.text: This makes a distinction clear: should the maker's listed burn time be judged by the spiral shape or by each product?

c05r087.text: I think this is the easiest mistake: confusing what the shape does with what the material does.

c05r088.text: For today's regular size, KINCHO lists one coil at about 75 centimeters, with a burn time of about 7 hours: a different generation of specifications.

c05r089.text: The maker also lists short- and long-duration sizes, and environmental conditions affect burn time. But is the inside still the old flower powder?

c05r090.text: Materials did not stop at early flower powder: the product in the maker's explanation uses synthetic pyrethroid active ingredients.

c05r091.text: Plant powder, wood flour and binders are still mixed in; a new active ingredient does not mean all plant material is gone.

c05rx005.text: The factory says the plant powders include what remains after pyrethrum's active ingredients are removed. It is not just pesticide.

c05rx006.text: But loose powder scatters. What can hold it in a spiral you can pick up?

c05rx007.text: The maker lists binding powders and starch, mixed with plant powder and active ingredients to make a workable material.

c05rx008.text: So materials also support the shape: you hold a circle, but the factory must first make powder hold its form.

c05r092.text: Make the mixture into a sheet, die-cut spirals and dry them: that is another method the factory page describes.

c05rx009.text: Think binding powder into a circle finishes the job? What must it release into the air as it burns?

c05rx010.text: As it burns, active ingredients enter the air as extremely fine particles; this too is how the maker describes it working.

c05rx011.text: So the powder must both hold a shape and keep burning. Only here do shape, material and time really connect.

c05r093.text: The hand-winding you saw earlier is replaced here by die-cutting. The circle remains; the way of making it changes.

c05r101.text: Back to the mold that never entered production: a spiral was only the idea's start. Material, making and delivery together make a product.

c05r102.text: If you've snapped a coil while separating a joined pair, tell me in the comments: did you grab the center or outer edge first?

c05r103.text: To explore the choices behind everyday objects that go beyond a single good idea, subscribe to this channel.
